prompt: Put the five questions of a security review in the lesson's order.
Why does 'who may do this?' come first?

choices.text: It is the quickest question to answer
choices.why: It is often the slowest, because the answer is a missing line.

choices.text: A missing check cannot be seen
choices.why: Right. It is invisible in the code that is there: the reviewer has to ask about the line that is absent, and the cost of missing it is other people's data.

choices.text: Linters already answer the other four
choices.why: Some, partly; lesson 19 says which.

choices.text: Authorisation bugs are the only security bugs
choices.why: The other four questions exist for a reason.

prompt: A new route calls a helper written last year. What does the lesson tell the reviewer to do?

choices.text: Trust it: it passed review last year
choices.why: It was reviewed for last year's callers, not this one.

choices.text: Open the old code
choices.why: Right. The flaw is often where a new line meets an unchanged one.

choices.text: Ask the author to rewrite the helper
choices.why: Maybe, after reading it; not before.

choices.text: Ignore it: only changed lines are in scope
choices.why: The change's behaviour includes what it calls.

prompt: Why does the lesson suggest reading the pull request's description last?

choices.text: Descriptions are usually wrong
choices.why: This one was entirely true.

choices.text: Reviewers should not talk to authors
choices.why: They should; comments are exactly that.

choices.text: It makes you see the intention instead of the code
choices.why: Right. The description says what was meant; the diff says what was done.

choices.text: It is shown below the diff by the tool
choices.why: Tools show it on top; the order is a choice.

prompt: How many new routes does the messages branch add?
Which command shows the change on the branch against main?

choices.text: git diff main messages
choices.why: Right. Every line that differs between the two.

choices.text: git log main
choices.why: That lists commits, not the change.

choices.text: git status
choices.why: That shows the working tree, not a branch.

choices.text: git init -b messages
choices.why: That creates a repository.

prompt: Every sentence of the pull request's description is true. Why is it still not a reason to approve?

choices.text: Descriptions should be longer
choices.why: Length would not help.

choices.text: It says what was meant
choices.why: Right. It describes what was meant, not what the change allows. 'Simplified the secret key' is true and hides finding 4.

choices.text: Only tests can approve a change
choices.why: People approve; tests help them.

choices.text: The description was written in English
choices.why: The language is not the issue.

prompt: Match each finding to the lesson that teaches its fix.

pairs.left: the sender chooses whose message it is

prompt: How does the reviewer propose keeping line breaks without trusting HTML?

choices.text:
Replace newlines with
before escaping
choices.why:
Then the
is escaped and shows as text.

choices.text: white-space: pre-line, text still escaped
choices.why: Right. No HTML needs to be trusted for a newline.

choices.text: Mark only the first message as safe
choices.why: Safe for one patient's text is still safe for a patient's text.

choices.text: Strip all newlines from messages
choices.why: That loses what the author wanted, and it is not needed.

prompt: Why is a secret key written in the code a security finding, not a style one?

choices.text: Strings in code are slower than random bytes
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Flask refuses short keys
choices.why: It accepts them, which is the problem.

choices.text: Repository readers could sign sessions
choices.why: Right. The server would accept those cookies as genuine.

choices.text: The key is too easy to remember
choices.why: Memorability is not the issue; where it is stored is.

prompt: `message.get("patient", patient())` falls back to the session. Why is that still a finding?

choices.text: Because patient() can raise an error
choices.why: That raise is the sign-in check working.

choices.text: The form's value wins whenever the form has one
choices.why: Right. The session is only a fallback, so the request decides whose message it is.

choices.text: dict() copies the form too slowly
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: get() is deprecated on dictionaries
choices.why: It is not.

prompt: Which of these did the reviewer mark as not blocking? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: two messages getting the same number
choices.why: Real, and it exposes nobody's data.

choices.text: a missing message number raising a 500
choices.why: Real, and below the six.

choices.text: any patient reading any message
choices.why: That one is first, and blocking.

choices.text: the secret key in the code
choices.why: Blocking: it lets sessions be produced by others.

prompt: Why can a comment asking for a test be worth more than one describing the fix?

choices.text: Tests are faster to write than fixes
choices.why: Not necessarily, and not the point.

choices.text: Authors ignore comments about code
choices.why: Not the argument the lesson makes.

choices.text: The test stays after the reviewer has gone
choices.why: Right. It fails loudly if the flaw ever comes back.

choices.text: Tests replace the need to fix
choices.why: A failing test still needs the fix.

prompt: Put the four parts of a comment that works in the lesson's order.
Which comment on finding 1 works best?

choices.text: Insecure.
choices.why: It starts an argument, not a fix.

choices.text: Every message is readable by any patient: no owner check in read_message. Answer 404 and add a test. Blocking.
choices.why: Right. What happens, evidence, a way out, how much it matters.

choices.text: Please review the security of every route, template and setting before opening any more pull requests on this repository.
choices.why: Nothing specific to act on.

choices.text: LGTM, but think about access control.
choices.why: An approval with a vague worry attached.

prompt: When should a reviewer ask a question rather than state a fact?

choices.text: Always, to sound polite
choices.why: A fact stated as a question hides how certain it is.

choices.text: Never; reviews should be assertive
choices.why: Some findings depend on what the author meant.

choices.text: When the finding depends on what the author meant
choices.why: Right. The answer may change the fix, as with a staff route sending on a patient's behalf.

choices.text: When the author is more senior
choices.why: Seniority does not change what the code does.

prompt: A reviewer approves with 'LGTM' without opening the template changes. What does the lesson say they should have done?

choices.text: Approved anyway; the author is responsible
choices.why: Approving is a statement the reviewer makes too.

choices.text: Said what they did not read
choices.why: Right. Approve what you read, and say what you did not check.

choices.text: Rejected the whole change
choices.why: Without reading it, a rejection says as little as the approval.

choices.text: Asked another reviewer to approve instead
choices.why: That moves the problem without saying it.

prompt: A comment that must be resolved before merging is marked as ___.
What can a checklist NOT do, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Remind the reviewer of known flaws
choices.why: That is exactly what it does.

choices.text: Find a flaw nobody listed
choices.why: Right. The five questions are for those, together with knowing the system.

choices.text: Fit on one screen
choices.why: This one does, on purpose.

choices.text: Be used on every review
choices.why: That is what a short one is for.

prompt: Which of these can a machine check before the review starts, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a pin that became a range
choices.why: A pattern in requirements.txt.

choices.text: a known advisory against a version
choices.why: pip-audit, from lesson 17.

choices.text: a template marked safe
choices.why: A pattern in the code.

choices.text: whether a message belongs to the caller
choices.why: That needs somebody who knows the system.

prompt: Why does a reviewer who knows the system see finding 1 at once?

choices.text: They have read the checklist more often
choices.why: The checklist alone shows a route that works.

choices.text: They know messages belong to patients
choices.why: Right. Knowing whose data it is turns a working route into a question.

choices.text: The route has an obvious syntax error
choices.why: It runs perfectly.

choices.text: A linter flags it
choices.why: No linter knows who owns a message.

prompt: A change adds `DELETE /bookings/<id>` with a sign-in check and nothing else, and its tests show a patient deleting their own booking. What is the first comment?

choices.text: Use PATCH to mark it cancelled instead of deleting the row
choices.why: A design point, worth making second.

choices.text: Ask whose it is, and for a test of the refusal
choices.why: Right. Add the owner check and a test that one patient cannot delete another's; the tests only show the case that works.

choices.text: Rename the route to /appointments
choices.why: Naming comes last.

choices.text: Add logging of every deletion
choices.why: Useful later; it does not stop the wrong deletion.

prompt: A diff changes only requirements.txt: `jinja2==3.1.6` becomes `jinja2==3.1.4`. What do you ask?

choices.text: Nothing; it is still pinned
choices.why: Pinned to a version with published advisories.

choices.text: Whether the team prefers Jinja2 or another engine
choices.why: Off topic for this change.

choices.text: Why it went backwards
choices.why: Right. And what the audit says now: lesson 17's audit found advisories fixed only in 3.1.5 and 3.1.6.

choices.text: To also downgrade Flask to match
choices.why: That would make it worse.

prompt: A review has twenty comments of equal weight. What is the risk?

choices.text: The two that matter are hidden among the rest
choices.why: Right. Mark the blocking ones and label the rest as suggestions.

choices.text: The review tool refuses more than ten
choices.why: No such limit.

choices.text: The author must answer them in order
choices.why: There is no required order.

choices.text: Twenty comments approve the change automatically
choices.why: Comments approve nothing.
